text: According to the General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) model, what is the immediate physiological response during the 'Alarm' phase following an acute bout of unaccustomed high-intensity resistance exercise?
options: Immediate upregulation of structural myofibrillar protein synthesis and satellite cell accretion
Temporary reduction in neuromuscular performance, acute stiffness, and structural microtrauma
Rapid supercompensation of muscle glycogen stores, neural facilitation, and peak power output
Long-term structural remodeling, increased connective tissue stiffness, and load desensitization
explanation: The Alarm phase of Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome is characterized by acute physiological disruption, soreness, stiffness, and a transient drop in neuromuscular performance before recovery and supercompensation occur.
source: Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning (NSCA) - G. Gregory Haff & N. Travis Triplett

text: When designing a resistance training program specifically for maximal strength development in an elite athlete, which load and repetition scheme is recommended by the NSCA?
options: Loads of ≥85% of 1RM performed for ≤6 repetitions per set with 2 to 5 minutes of rest
Loads of ≤67% of 1RM performed for 12 to 20 repetitions per set with 30 to 60 seconds of rest
Loads of 67% to 85% of 1RM performed for 8 to 12 repetitions per set with 1 to 2 minutes of rest
Loads of 75% to 80% of 1RM performed for 15 to 25 repetitions per set with active recovery rest
explanation: For maximal strength development, the NSCA guidelines recommend using loads of 85% of 1RM or greater with 6 or fewer repetitions per set, accompanied by 2 to 5 minutes of rest between sets.
source: Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning (NSCA) - G. Gregory Haff & N. Travis Triplett

text: In velocity-based training (VBT), a barbell velocity loss exceeding 30% during a resistance set is primarily indicative of which physiological state?
options: Rapid phosphocreatine replenishment facilitating elevated motor unit firing synchronization
Substantial neuromuscular fatigue accumulation, intracellular acidosis, and reduced power
Optimal accumulation of mechanical strain required for high-velocity tendon adaptation
Selective recruitment of high-threshold Type IIx motor units without metabolic accumulation
explanation: In velocity-based training, velocity loss greater than 30-40% indicates significant neuromuscular and central fatigue with high metabolic accumulation, making it inappropriate for power-specific sessions.
source: Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning (NSCA) - G. Gregory Haff & N. Travis Triplett

text: During the stretch-shortening cycle (SSC) in plyometric training, what is the critical physiological role of minimizing the duration of the 'amortization' phase?
options: Preserving stored elastic energy in series elastic components and optimizing stretch reflex drive
Allowing Golgi tendon organ Ib afferents to inhibit alpha motor neuron excitability completely
Preventing the premature recruitment of fast-twitch motor units in distal lower limb musculature
Maximizing the thermal dissipation of stored elastic strain energy prior to the concentric phase
explanation: The amortization phase is the electromechanical delay between the eccentric and concentric phases. Minimizing its duration prevents the dissipation of stored strain energy as heat and maximizes reflex potentiation.
source: Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning (NSCA) - G. Gregory Haff & N. Travis Triplett

text: What is the primary factor limiting oxygen delivery and VO2max in healthy, well-trained endurance athletes exercising at sea level?
options: Intracellular myoglobin concentration and rate of sarcolemmal glucose transporter translocation
Maximal stroke volume, cardiac output, and peripheral capillary vascular perfusion
Maximal mitochondrial oxidative enzyme concentration within slow-twitch skeletal muscle
Pulmonary alveolar-capillary membrane diffusion capacity and mechanical lung compliance
explanation: In healthy endurance athletes at sea level, the primary rate-limiting step for VO2max is central cardiovascular oxygen transport capacity (maximal cardiac output / stroke volume), rather than pulmonary diffusion or peripheral oxidative enzymes.
source: Exercise Physiology: Nutrition, Energy, and Human Performance - McArdle, Katch & Katch

text: During high-intensity sprint exercise, the depletion of which intracellular substrate corresponds most directly with rapid muscular fatigue during the initial 10 seconds of maximal effort?
options: Intramuscular triacylglycerol stores within oxidative Type I motor units
Subcutaneous adipose tissue fatty acid reserves mobilized via beta-oxidation
Hepatic glycogen stores utilized for circulating blood glucose maintenance
Phosphocreatine stores required for immediate rephosphorylation of ADP to ATP
explanation: During all-out maximal exertion lasting up to 10 seconds, phosphocreatine (PCr) depletion is the primary limiting factor causing immediate declines in maximal anaerobic power output.
source: Exercise Physiology: Nutrition, Energy, and Human Performance - McArdle, Katch & Katch

text: What causes the rightward shift of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve (Bohr Effect) during intense muscular exercise?
options: Decreased 2,3-diphosphoglycerate concentration and reduced metabolic rate
Increased arterial PO2, increased cellular bicarbonate, and elevated blood pH
Increased blood temperature, increased blood PCO2, and decreased arterial pH
Decreased core temperature, decreased blood PCO2, and increased blood pH
explanation: The Bohr effect is a rightward shift of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve caused by elevated temperature, elevated PCO2, elevated 2,3-DPG, and reduced pH (increased H+), facilitating oxygen unloading to exercising muscles.
source: Exercise Physiology - Kenney, Wilmore & Costill

text: Which sensory receptor is primarily responsible for detecting rapid changes in muscle length and triggering the myotatic (stretch) reflex?
options: 1.2 to 2.0 grams per kilogram of body weight per day to support muscle repair and growth
0.4 to 0.6 grams per kilogram of body weight per day to prevent renal nitrogen accumulation
3.5 to 4.5 grams per kilogram of body weight per day to replace all dietary carbohydrates
5.0 to 6.0 grams per kilogram of body weight per day to induce continuous ketogenesis
explanation: Muscle spindles are stretch receptors arranged in parallel with extrafusal fibers that detect the magnitude and rate of change in muscle length, triggering the monosynaptic stretch reflex via Ia sensory afferents.
source: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann

text: What type of lever system is exemplified by the triceps brachii extending the elbow against resistance, and what is its mechanical characteristic?
options: Fourth-Class Lever, where mechanical advantage always exceeds two for high force amplification
Second-Class Lever, where the load resistance lies between the fulcrum and the effort force
First-Class Lever, where the fulcrum lies between the effort force and the load resistance
Third-Class Lever, where the effort force is applied between the fulcrum and the load resistance
explanation: Elbow extension by the triceps is a classic First-Class lever: the fulcrum (elbow joint axis) lies between the applied effort force (triceps tendon insertion on the olecranon) and the resistance load.
source: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann

text: In force-plate biomechanical analysis, how is the vertical ground reaction force (vGRF) impulse calculated during the propulsive phase of a vertical jump?
options: By determining the second derivative of the vertical velocity curve over time
By calculating the time integral of the vertical ground reaction force curve
By multiplying the maximum jump displacement by the athlete's total body mass
By dividing the peak vertical ground reaction force by total jump movement time
explanation: Impulse is defined as the product of force and time, calculated mathematically as the area under the force-time curve (the integral of force with respect to time), directly determining changes in linear momentum.
source: Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning (NSCA) - G. Gregory Haff & N. Travis Triplett

text: During an incremental exercise test, the blood lactate threshold (LT1) is generally identified when blood lactate concentration first exhibits what behavior?
options: Reaches a fixed absolute threshold of 8.0 mmol/L during high-intensity cycling
Drops below resting baseline levels due to rapid hepatic gluconeogenesis clearance
Demonstrates a sustained initial rise of ≥1.0 mmol/L above resting baseline values
Stabilizes at a steady plateau of 4.0 mmol/L regardless of incremental workload
explanation: Lactate Threshold 1 (LT1 / Aerobic Threshold) is standardly defined as the exercise intensity at which blood lactate first begins to rise systematically above resting baseline levels (typically ~2.0 mmol/L or a sustained 1.0 mmol/L increase).
source: Exercise Physiology: Nutrition, Energy, and Human Performance - McArdle, Katch & Katch

text: What is the recommended daily protein intake range for elite athletes aiming to maximize muscle protein synthesis during intense resistance training periods?
options: 0.2 to 0.4 g/kg body weight per day supplemented with branched-chain amino acids
3.5 to 4.5 g/kg body weight per day consumed exclusively before bedtime
0.6 to 0.8 g/kg body weight per day distributed across two large meals
1.4 to 2.0 g/kg body weight per day distributed evenly across 3 to 5 meals
explanation: The International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) and ACSM position stands recommend 1.4 to 2.0 g/kg/day for exercising individuals to optimize muscle protein synthesis and recovery, spaced evenly every 3 to 4 hours.
source: Sports Nutrition - Asker Jeukendrup & Michael Gleeson

text: What is the primary physiological mechanism explaining the ergogenic benefit of Beta-Alanine supplementation in high-intensity sports lasting 1 to 4 minutes?
options: Expanding intravascular plasma volume to enhance peripheral thermoregulatory cooling
Stimulating direct central nervous system dopamine release to delay central fatigue
Accelerating mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation during submaximal exercise
Increasing intracellular intramuscular carnosine synthesis to buffer proton accumulation
explanation: Beta-alanine is the rate-limiting precursor to carnosine. Daily supplementation elevates muscle carnosine content, enhancing intracellular H+ buffering capacity during high-intensity anaerobic exercise lasting 60–240 seconds.
source: Sports Nutrition - Asker Jeukendrup & Michael Gleeson

text: According to ISAK anthropometry standards, which anatomical landmarks define the measurement of the Medial Calf skinfold?
options: The distal third of the medial gastrocnemius muscle belly near the Achilles junction
The posterior midline of the calf at the level of maximal calf circumference
The medial aspect of the calf at the level of maximal calf circumference
The anterior tibial tuberosity midpoint at the level of minimal shank girth
explanation: The ISAK medial calf skinfold site is located on the medial aspect of the calf, at the level of maximal calf circumference, with the subject standing relaxed and weight evenly distributed.
source: Kinanthropometry and Exercise Physiology - Roger Eston & Thomas Reilly

text: In the Heath-Carter somatotype classification system, what phenotypic characteristic is quantified by the 'Ectomorphy' component?
options: Relative trunk volume, abdominal circumference, and visceral organ mass
Relative musculoskeletal robusticity and skeletal bone breadth relative to stature
Relative subcutaneous adiposity and total body fat mass relative to height
Relative linearity, slenderness, and delicate skeletal frame relative to stature
explanation: In the Heath-Carter somatotype method, Ectomorphy describes relative linearity and slenderness of an individual, calculated from the height-to-weight ratio (HWR = height / cube root of mass).
source: Kinanthropometry and Exercise Physiology - Roger Eston & Thomas Reilly

text: According to the Individual Zones of Optimal Functioning (IZOF) theory in sports psychology (Yuri Hanin), how does pre-competition anxiety relate to performance?
options: Every athlete performs best at an identical moderate level of state anxiety
Each athlete possesses an individualized bandwidth of optimal anxiety for peak output
Anxiety always impairs athletic performance in a direct negative linear fashion
Pre-competition anxiety has zero correlation with motor skill execution or cognitive focus
explanation: Hanin's IZOF model posits that optimal emotional arousal/anxiety is idiosyncratic: some athletes perform best at high anxiety, others at moderate, and others at low anxiety zones.
source: Foundations of Sport and Exercise Psychology - Robert S. Weinberg & Daniel Gould

text: Which Heart Rate Variability (HRV) time-domain index is most widely used to track cardiac parasympathetic (vagal) activity and athletic recovery status?
options: 0.01 grams per kilogram body weight once weekly, followed by zero long-term maintenance intake
5.0 grams per kilogram body weight per day continuously throughout the entire competitive season
1.5 grams per kilogram body weight per day for 30 days, followed by 0.50–0.80 g/kg/day maintenance
0.3 grams per kilogram body weight per day for 5–7 days, followed by 0.03–0.05 g/kg/day maintenance
explanation: RMSSD reflects beat-to-beat parasympathetic regulation of the heart rate. A decrease in RMSSD typically signals autonomic fatigue, excessive physiological stress, or incomplete recovery.
source: Monitoring Training and Performance in Athletes - Mike McGuigan

text: In clinical research biostatistics, what does the 'Intraclass Correlation Coefficient' (ICC) primarily evaluate?
options: The relative reliability and test-retest consistency of continuous measurement scales
The proportion of variance explained by a multiple linear regression model
The statistical significance of differences between two independent sample means
The linear cause-and-effect relationship between an exposure and an outcome variable
explanation: The Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) is the gold-standard reliability index reflecting both degree of correlation and agreement between repeated measurements taken by the same or different raters.
source: Foundations of Clinical Research: Applications to Practice - Leslie G. Portney

text: In clinical diagnostic testing, what does a high 'Sensitivity' indicate regarding a physical assessment test?
options: The test produces zero false positive results across all screened patient cohorts
The test results remain completely unchanged across repeated multi-center evaluations
The test accurately identifies a high proportion of individuals who truly have the condition
The test accurately identifies all healthy individuals who do not possess the condition
explanation: Sensitivity is the true positive rate (TP / [TP + FN]). A highly sensitive test rarely misses individuals with the condition, making a negative result highly useful for ruling out pathology (SnNout).
source: Foundations of Clinical Research: Applications to Practice - Leslie G. Portney

text: What is the primary physiological mechanism by which 'Pranayama' (slow yogic breathing at ~6 breaths per minute) enhances athletic autonomic recovery?
options: Activating pulmonary stretch receptors and arterial baroreflexes to increase vagal tone
Stimulating sympathetic vasomotor efferents to elevate mean arterial blood pressure
Inducing mild cerebral hypocapnia to stimulate respiratory motor unit firing rates
Suppressing renal renin secretion to lower circulating plasma blood volume
explanation: Slow paced breathing at ~0.1 Hz (6 breaths/min) stimulates pulmonary stretch afferents and aligns with the intrinsic baroreflex frequency (resonance frequency), maximizing HRV and parasympathetic vagal reactivation.
source: Foundations of Sport and Exercise Psychology - Robert S. Weinberg & Daniel Gould

text: What is the definition of Low Energy Availability (LEA) in female athletes that serves as the primary etiology of the Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S) syndrome?
options: Energy Intake minus Exercise Energy Expenditure < 30 kcal/kg Fat-Free Mass/day
Total Daily Energy Intake < 2000 kcal/day regardless of body composition
Energy Intake minus Basal Metabolic Rate < 45 kcal/kg Total Body Mass/day
Carbohydrate Intake < 3 g/kg Total Body Mass/day during high-volume training
explanation: Energy Availability (EA) is defined as (Energy Intake - Exercise Energy Expenditure) / Fat-Free Mass. An EA below 30 kcal/kg FFM/day represents the critical threshold triggering neuroendocrine and metabolic disruptions in RED-S.
source: Sports Nutrition - Asker Jeukendrup & Michael Gleeson / IOC Consensus

text: When an elite sports team travels eastward across more than six time zones, which circadian phase-shifting protocol is recommended to accelerate adaptation?
options: Avoiding all natural sunlight exposure for the first seven days following international arrival
Seeking bright light exposure in the late evening and delaying morning wake-up times
Maintaining home time-zone sleeping schedules and avoiding all physical activity in mornings
Seeking bright light exposure in the morning and taking low-dose melatonin in the evening
explanation: Eastward travel requires phase-advancing the circadian clock: morning bright light exposure (to shift the circadian rhythm earlier) combined with evening exogenous melatonin facilitates rapid resynchronization.
source: Monitoring Training and Performance in Athletes - Mike McGuigan

text: Under the World Anti-Doping Code, which physiological mechanism explains why autologous blood transfusion is classified as a strictly prohibited doping method (M1)?
options: Inhibits peripheral pain receptors to allow supramaximal anaerobic lactic acid accumulation
Suppresses endogenous erythropoietin secretion to induce acute systemic hemodilution
Directly stimulates myocellular hypertrophy by activating insulin-like growth factor pathways
Artificially elevates total red blood cell mass and arterial oxygen-carrying capacity
explanation: Autologous blood transfusion artificially expands total hemoglobin mass and circulating erythrocyte volume, increasing maximal oxygen delivery (VO2max) and aerobic endurance, violating WADA Category M1.
source: WADA International Standard Prohibited List / NADA India

text: In high-performance sports programs, what is the primary objective of an integrated multidisciplinary Performance Support Team (PST)?
options: Ensuring each sport science discipline operates in complete isolation to prevent protocol overlap
Limiting athlete training loads to strictly submaximal intensities across the entire season
Replacing sport-specific coaching staff with clinical exercise physiology specialists
Aligning biomechanics, physiology, physiotherapy, and nutrition to optimize athlete availability
explanation: A high-performance interdisciplinary team integrates sports medicine, physiotherapy, strength & conditioning, physiology, and nutrition into a unified, athlete-centered system optimizing readiness and performance.
source: Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning (NSCA) - G. Gregory Haff & N. Travis Triplett

text: In training load management, what does an Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio (ACWR) between 0.80 and 1.30 represent according to Tim Gabbett's workload-injury model?
options: The 'Under-training Zone', where athlete fitness drops and injury vulnerability increases
The 'Danger Zone', where rapid workload spikes significantly increase soft-tissue injury risk
The 'Sweet Spot', where training loads build fitness while minimizing soft-tissue injury risk
The 'Overreaching Zone', where chronic fatigue exceeds the physiological recovery ceiling
explanation: Tim Gabbett's ACWR model defines the 0.80–1.30 range as the optimal training 'sweet spot' where the acute load is safely matched to chronic fitness, reducing relative injury risk compared to spikes ≥1.50.
source: Monitoring Training and Performance in Athletes - Mike McGuigan / Gabbett

text: In wearable GPS athlete tracking technology, what physical metric is quantified by 'PlayerLoad' (or Dynamic Stress Load)?
options: The instantaneous tri-axial accelerometry vector magnitude of movement across 3 planes
The total distance traveled above 25 km/h during high-intensity competitive match play
The metabolic equivalent of task (MET) estimated from integrated telemetry heart rate
The peak mechanical impact force experienced by the plantar fascia during ground contact
explanation: PlayerLoad (developed by Catapult) is calculated as the square root of the sum of the squared instantaneous rates of change in acceleration across three orthogonal axes (x, y, and z), sampled at 100 Hz.
source: Monitoring Training and Performance in Athletes - Mike McGuigan

text: In musculoskeletal injury surveillance, how is the 'Injury Incidence Rate' standardly quantified according to international consensus (Fuller et al.)?
options: Total financial expenditure on medical rehabilitation divided by total squad players
Number of injuries per 1,000 player-hours of sports exposure (training and match play)
Number of injuries per 100 registered athletes over an entire four-year Olympic cycle
Percentage of squad athletes absent from training on any single randomized calendar day
explanation: The international consensus on sports injury epidemiology (IOC/FIFA/World Rugby) defines injury incidence as the number of injuries per 1,000 hours of athlete exposure, differentiating match and training incidence.
source: Foundations of Clinical Research: Applications to Practice - Leslie G. Portney / Fuller et al.

text: What is the primary cellular mechanism by which local Cold-Water Immersion (CWI at 10–15°C for 10–15 min) immediately post-exercise reduces acute delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS)?
options: Accelerating blood lactate clearance by converting circulating lactate into structural collagen
Directly stimulating satellite cell proliferation and structural myofibrillar protein synthesis
Promoting cutaneous vasoconstriction, reducing microvascular permeability and inflammatory edema
Inducing profound arterial vasodilation to accelerate intramuscular glycogen synthesis
explanation: Cold-water immersion causes local vasoconstriction, which decreases capillary permeability, reduces fluid extravasation and neutrophil infiltration, blunting acute secondary inflammatory muscle edema and soreness.
source: Monitoring Training and Performance in Athletes - Mike McGuigan

text: In sports nutrition, what is the primary rationale for co-ingesting carbohydrates with protein during the immediate post-exercise recovery window?
options: Carbohydrates directly convert dietary amino acids into structural cross-linked collagen fibrils
Carbohydrates neutralize blood lactic acid by binding directly to free circulating hydrogen ions
Carbohydrates suppress gastric emptying rates to prolong amino acid absorption over 24 hours
Carbohydrates stimulate insulin secretion, which enhances cellular amino acid uptake and glycogen storage
explanation: Carbohydrate intake elevates circulating insulin, an anabolic hormone that stimulates muscle glycogen synthase activity, increases amino acid transport into myocytes, and suppresses post-exercise muscle proteolysis.
source: Sports Nutrition - Asker Jeukendrup & Michael Gleeson

text: In biomechanics, what is the mechanical definition of 'Torque' (Moment of Force) acting around a human joint axis?
options: The total mechanical work completed divided by the time duration of muscular contraction
The linear rate of change of momentum along the longitudinal anatomical axis of a limb
The second derivative of angular displacement with respect to the radius of gyration
The cross product of the applied force vector and the perpendicular moment arm distance
explanation: Torque ($	au = F 	imes d_\perp$) is the rotary effect of a force, calculated as the magnitude of the applied force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the line of action to the joint axis of rotation.
source: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann

text: During non-contact deceleration and sidestep cutting tasks in field sports, which biomechanical triad significantly increases peak anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tensile strain?
options: Shallow knee flexion (<30°), dynamic knee valgus moment, and internal tibial/hip rotation
Neutral sagittal knee alignment, ankle dorsiflexion >20°, and upright trunk posture
Deep knee flexion (>60°), hip external rotation, and wide base of support at initial contact
Posterior trunk lean, symmetrical bilateral foot contact, and active hamstring co-contraction
explanation: Extensive 3D biomechanical research identifies shallow knee flexion (<30°), dynamic knee valgus (abduction moment), and internal hip rotation/tibial rotation as the high-risk multiplanar mechanism loading the ACL.
source: Brukner & Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine - Peter Brukner et al. / Hewett

text: In athlete monitoring, what is the primary diagnostic utility of the 'Countermovement Jump' (CMJ) test performed on dual force plates?
options: A heavy open-chain leg extension program performed strictly with maximal 1RM resistance loads
A 6-month continuous passive motorized stretching regimen performed exclusively on massage tables
An 8-week structured neuromuscular training program incorporating plyometrics and landing mechanics
A complete bed rest protocol with strict immobilization of both lower extremities in rigid casts
explanation: Dual force plate CMJ testing provides comprehensive neuromuscular profiling: jump height, eccentric deceleration impulse, concentric propulsive power, and dynamic inter-limb force asymmetries.
source: Monitoring Training and Performance in Athletes - Mike McGuigan

text: Under the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports (MYAS), what is the primary objective of the Target Olympic Podium Scheme (TOPS)?
options: Target Olympic Podium Scheme (TOPS - providing specialized elite funding)
National Sports Development Fund (NSDF - public corporate sports fund)
Khelo India Youth Games (KIYG - national grassroots talent competition)
Mission Olympic Cell (MOC - apex body evaluating elite athlete support)
explanation: The Target Olympic Podium Scheme (TOPS), launched by MYAS in 2014, identifies and provides comprehensive customized support (coaching, foreign exposure, equipment, sports science, and ₹50,000/month stipend) to elite Olympic and Paralympic medal prospects.
source: Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports (MYAS) Official Portal / TOPS Guidelines

text: What is the official motto of the Olympic Games as updated by the International Olympic Committee (IOC) in 2021?
options: Citius, Altius, Fortius – Perpetuo (Faster, Higher, Stronger – Permanently)
Citius, Altius, Fortius – Concorditer (Faster, Higher, Stronger – In Harmony)
Citius, Altius, Fortius – Fideliter (Faster, Higher, Stronger – Faithfully)
Citius, Altius, Fortius – Communiter (Faster, Higher, Stronger – Together)
explanation: In July 2021, the IOC Session approved updating the historic Olympic motto to 'Citius, Altius, Fortius – Communiter' (Latin for 'Faster, Higher, Stronger – Together') to emphasize global solidarity.
source: International Olympic Committee (IOC) Official Records

text: Which statutory autonomous body is responsible for promoting, coordinating, and monitoring the anti-doping program in sports across India under the National Anti-Doping Act, 2022?
options: National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA India - statutory national body)
Indian Olympic Association (IOA - national Olympic committee body)
Sports Authority of India (SAI - apex sports development authority)
National Dope Testing Laboratory (NDTL - WADA accredited testing lab)
explanation: NADA India is the national statutory body established under central legislation to implement WADA-compliant anti-doping rules, testing, education, and results management across all sports in India.
source: National Anti-Doping Act, 2022 / NADA India Official Portal

text: Which city will host the Games of the XXXIV Olympiad (2028 Summer Olympic and Paralympic Games)?
options: Madrid, Community of Madrid, Spain (Candidate Olympic host city)
Los Angeles, California, USA (2028 Summer Olympic Games host)
Paris, Île-de-France, France (2024 Summer Olympic Games host city)
Brisbane, Queensland, Australia (2032 Summer Olympic Games host)
explanation: The 2028 Summer Olympic and Paralympic Games will be hosted by Los Angeles, California, USA (LA 2028), following Paris 2024 and preceding Brisbane 2032.
source: International Olympic Committee (IOC) Official Records

text: Under the National Sports Development Code of India (2011), what is the maximum age limit prescribed for an individual holding the post of President in a National Sports Federation (NSF)?
options: 75 years of age
70 years of age
65 years of age
60 years of age
explanation: The National Sports Development Code of India (2011) mandates that NSF office bearers (President, Secretary, Treasurer) cannot contest elections upon attaining the age of 70 years.
source: National Sports Development Code of India (2011) - MYAS

text: What is the highest sporting honor awarded annually in India by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports?
options: Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna Award (Highest sporting honour in India)
Rashtriya Khel Protsahan Puruskar (Sports promotion and development)
Dronacharya Award for Outstanding Coaches (Premier coach recognition)
Arjuna Award for Outstanding Performance (Premier sports recognition)
explanation: The Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna Award (instituted in 1991–92, renamed in 2021) is India's highest national sports award, carrying a medallion, certificate, and cash prize of ₹25 lakh.
source: Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports (MYAS) Scheme Guidelines

text: Where is the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS / TAS) headquartered?
options: Lausanne, Switzerland
Monaco City, Monaco
Geneva, Switzerland
Zurich, Switzerland
explanation: The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) is an independent international judicial body established in 1984, headquartered in Lausanne, Switzerland, to settle sports-related legal disputes.
source: Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) Official Statutes

text: Under the World Anti-Doping Code, what constitutes a 'Whereabouts Failure' by an athlete in a Registered Testing Pool (RTP)?
options: Any combination of three missed tests or filing failures within a 12-month period
Refusing to participate in a scheduled national championship tournament match
Failing to declare an over-the-counter dietary protein powder on a medical log
Traveling internationally without obtaining prior written approval from an NSF
explanation: Under WADA Code Article 2.4, any combination of three Filing Failures and/or Missed Tests within a rolling 12-month period by an athlete in a Registered Testing Pool constitutes an Anti-Doping Rule Violation (ADRV).
source: World Anti-Doping Code / NADA India Guidelines

text: Which orthopedic special test is recognized as the most sensitive physical examination maneuver for diagnosing an acute Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) tear?
options: Pivot-Shift Test performed with valgus and internal rotation
Anterior Drawer Test performed at 90 degrees of knee flexion
Apley Compression Test performed in the prone position
Lachman Test performed at 20 to 30 degrees of knee flexion
explanation: The Lachman test (20–30° flexion) has the highest sensitivity (>95%) for acute ACL tears because the posterior horns of the menisci do not wedge against the femoral condyles and hamstring spasm is minimized.
source: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee

text: When performing the 'Pivot-Shift Test' for anterolateral knee rotatory instability, what anatomical event produces the characteristic palpable 'clunk' as the knee is flexed from extension?
options: The patella dislocating laterally over the elevated lateral femoral trochlear ridge during forced active knee extension at thirty degrees
The iliotibial band transitioning from extensor to flexor, spontaneously reducing the anteriorly subluxated lateral tibial plateau
The medial meniscus posterior horn snapping over the medial tibial spine margin during passive valgus stress and internal rotation
The posterior cruciate ligament subluxating behind the medial femoral condyle during active terminal extension of the tibiofemoral joint
explanation: In an ACL-deficient knee, the tibia starts subluxated anteriorly in extension; as the knee is flexed with valgus and internal rotation, the IT band switches at 30–40° from an extensor to a flexor, forcibly reducing the lateral tibial plateau.
source: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee

text: The 'Dial Test' (Tibial External Rotation Test) is performed at 30 degrees and 90 degrees of knee flexion. Increased external rotation of >10 degrees at 30 degrees ONLY (normal at 90 degrees) indicates isolated injury to which structure?
options: Posterolateral Corner (PLC) complex without a concomitant PCL tear
Superficial Medial Collateral Ligament and posterior oblique ligament
Combined Posterior Cruciate Ligament and Posterolateral Corner disruption
Anterior Cruciate Ligament anteromedial and posterolateral bundle tear
explanation: At 30° flexion, the PLC (LCL, popliteus tendon, popliteofibular ligament) is isolated; at 90° flexion, the intact PCL secondary restraint checks rotation. Increased rotation at 30° only confirms isolated PLC injury.
source: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee

text: Which clinical physical examination test has the highest diagnostic accuracy for identifying subacromial impingement syndrome when combined in a cluster with the Painful Arc and Infraspinatus muscle test?
options: Infraspinatus muscle tendon unit (posterior cuff strain)
Supraspinatus muscle tendon unit (subacromial impingement)
Teres Minor muscle tendon unit (external rotator tear)
Subscapularis muscle tendon unit (anterior instability)
explanation: Park et al. and Magee established that the Hawkins-Kennedy test, Painful Arc sign, and Infraspinatus muscle test form the highest-yield diagnostic cluster for subacromial impingement (positive likelihood ratio > 10.5).
source: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee

text: The 'Crank Test' and 'O'Brien's Active Compression Test' of the glenohumeral joint are primarily designed to evaluate which structural pathology?
options: Acetabular Labral Tear or Femoroacetabular Impingement (FAI syndrome)
Greater Trochanteric Pain Syndrome or gluteal tendinopathy lesion
Iliopsoas bursitis with external snapping hip syndrome friction
Piriformis syndrome with sciatic nerve compression in the buttock
explanation: Both O'Brien's active compression test and the Crank test apply compression and rotational shear across the glenoid labrum, stressing the superior labrum-biceps anchor complex to detect SLAP lesions.
source: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee

text: The 'Finkelstein Test' is diagnostic for de Quervain's Tenosynovitis when ulnar deviation of the wrist with the thumb flexed inside the fist reproduces sharp pain in which anatomical structure?
options: Gluteus medius insertional tendinopathy at the greater trochanter
Femoral neck stress fracture with cortical bone displacement risk
Iliopsoas muscle strain with retroperitoneal bursal inflammation
Sacroiliac joint dysfunction or anterior sacroiliac ligament pathology
explanation: Finkelstein's test stretches the tendons of the first dorsal compartment of the wrist (Abductor Pollicis Longus and Extensor Pollicis Brevis) over the radial styloid, reproducing severe local pain in de Quervain's tenosynovitis.
source: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee

text: The 'FABER' (Patrick's) test places the tested lower extremity in Flexion, Abduction, and External Rotation. Pain localized strictly to the posterior sacroiliac region during downward overpressure indicates pathology in:
options: Posterior talofibular ligament deep capsular avulsion sprain
Deltoid ligament anterior superficial tibiotalar band strain
Anterior Talofibular Ligament (ATFL) complete or partial tear
Calcaneofibular Ligament (CFL) complete or partial rupture
explanation: FABER (Flexion, ABduction, External Rotation) stresses the ipsilateral anterior hip capsule and sacroiliac joint. Posterior SI joint pain indicates sacroiliac dysfunction, whereas groin pain indicates intra-articular hip pathology.
source: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee

text: During neurodynamic evaluation, the 'Slump Test' is considered positive for dural / neural tension when radicular leg symptoms reproduced during cervical and thoracic flexion are relieved by which maneuver?
options: Internally rotating the hip while maintaining knee extension
Extending the cervical spine while maintaining all other slump positions
Applying passive overpressure into greater ankle dorsiflexion
Increasing lumbar spine flexion toward the examination table
explanation: Structural differentiation is the hallmark of neurodynamic testing: if distal leg pain is altered by moving a distant proximal segment (releasing cervical flexion), a neurogenic/dural source is confirmed.
source: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee / Butler

text: In the DeLorme progressive resistance exercise (PRE) protocol, what percentage of the athlete's 10-Repetition Maximum (10RM) is lifted during Set 1, Set 2, and Set 3?
options: Set 1: 33% of 10RM, Set 2: 66% of 10RM, Set 3: 100% of 10RM
Set 1: 50% of 10RM, Set 2: 50% of 10RM, Set 3: 50% of 10RM
Set 1: 100% of 10RM, Set 2: 75% of 10RM, Set 3: 50% of 10RM
Set 1: 50% of 10RM, Set 2: 75% of 10RM, Set 3: 100% of 10RM
explanation: The classic DeLorme progressive loading protocol uses a built-in warm-up: Set 1 = 10 reps @ 50% 10RM, Set 2 = 10 reps @ 75% 10RM, and Set 3 = 10 reps @ 100% 10RM (whereas Oxford uses regressive loading).
source: Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques - Carolyn Kisner & Lynn Allen Colby

text: In tendinopathy rehabilitation, what is the Heavy Slow Resistance (HSR) protocol developed by Kongsgaard et al., and how does it compare to Alfredson's isolated eccentric loading?
options: Alfredson protocol: 3 sets of 15 repetitions, twice daily for 12 weeks, with the knee straight (Gastrocnemius) and knee bent (Soleus)
Heavy Slow Resistance protocol: 3 sets of 6–8 reps, 3 times weekly for 12 weeks, performed exclusively with maximum isokinetic devices
Silbernagel protocol: Concentric-eccentric loading with pain-guided activity, progressing to high-speed energy storage plyometrics
Stanish-Curwin protocol: Progressive eccentric loading with daily static stretching, increasing speed from slow to fast each week
explanation: Kongsgaard's HSR protocol involves bilateral/unilateral loading (e.g., squats/leg press) using 3–4 sets of 6–15RM with slow 3s eccentric and 3s concentric tempos 3 days per week, producing equivalent collagen remodeling to Alfredson's protocol.
source: Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques - Carolyn Kisner & Lynn Allen Colby / Kongsgaard

text: In manual therapy according to Maitland, what defines a 'Grade IV' joint mobilization technique?
options: A large-amplitude rhythmic oscillation performed within the pain-free beginning range
A high-velocity, low-amplitude thrust manipulation performed past the anatomical barrier
A sustained static distraction force applied perpendicular to the treatment plane for 60 seconds
A small-amplitude rhythmic oscillation performed at the very end of available joint range
explanation: Maitland Grade IV is a small-amplitude oscillatory movement performed right at the end of the available range of movement (moving into tissue resistance), designed to increase joint mobility and stretch periarticular stiffness.
source: Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques - Carolyn Kisner & Lynn Allen Colby

text: In Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation (PNF), which neurophysiological principle explains why a maximum isometric contraction of an antagonist muscle facilitates subsequent relaxation and greater passive stretch in that same muscle?
options: Gamma motor neuron loop sensitization increasing extrafusal fiber stiffness
Reciprocal Inhibition mediated by muscle spindle Ia inhibitory interneurons
Autogenic Inhibition mediated by Golgi tendon organ Ib afferent discharge
Spatial Summation of descending corticospinal motor unit action potentials
explanation: Contract-Relax and Hold-Relax PNF stretching techniques utilize Autogenic Inhibition: the high tension generated during the isometric contraction fires Golgi Tendon Organ Ib afferents, inhibiting the alpha motor neuron pool of that same muscle.
source: Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques - Carolyn Kisner & Lynn Allen Colby

text: In the McKenzie Method (Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy - MDT), what is the phenomenon of 'Centralization'?
options: The permanent loss of segmental spinal mobility following high-velocity low-amplitude thrust manipulation to the lower back
The gradual spread of pain from the lumbar spine down into the distal extremities during repetitive directional movement testing
The development of bilateral protective muscle spasm in response to prolonged static positioning in end-range spinal flexion
The progressive abolition of distal radiating symptoms toward the midline of the spine with repeated directional loading movements
explanation: Centralization is the rapid retreat and abolition of distal referred/radicular pain toward the lumbar or cervical midline in response to specific repeated mechanical movements (e.g., extension), indicating a reducible derangement.
source: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Conditions - Prof. P.P. Mohanty / McKenzie

text: According to Kaltenborn's 'Convex-Concave Rule', when a convex joint surface moves on a fixed concave surface, in what direction do the roll and glide (slide) occur?
options: Gliding occurs without any angular rolling across surfaces
Roll occurs normally while gliding translation is absent
Roll and glide occur in the exact same spatial direction
Roll and glide occur in opposite spatial directions always
explanation: Kaltenborn's rule: When a convex surface moves on a fixed concave surface (e.g., glenohumeral joint), bone roll and joint slide occur in OPPOSITE directions. When a concave surface moves on a convex surface, roll and slide occur in the SAME direction.
source: Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques - Carolyn Kisner & Lynn Allen Colby / Kaltenborn

text: In kinesiology, what is the 'Open-Packed' (Loose-Packed) resting position of the Glenohumeral joint?
options: Full adduction across the chest with maximal internal rotation behind the back
55 degrees of abduction and 30 degrees of horizontal adduction (scapular plane)
Full abduction and maximal external rotation in the 90/90 overhead position
90 degrees of pure abduction in the frontal plane with neutral rotation
explanation: The loose-packed position of the glenohumeral joint is ~55° abduction and 30° horizontal adduction (in the plane of the scapula), where capsuloligamentous structures are most relaxed and joint play is maximal.
source: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann

text: During normal human walking gait, what is the primary function of the 'First Ankle Rocker' (Heel Rocker) during the Initial Contact to Loading Response phase?
options: Decelerating the foot drop via eccentric contraction of the pretibial dorsiflexors and drawing the tibia forward over the heel rocker
Providing a rigid lever for explosive push-off during terminal stance transition by engaging the plantar aponeurosis mechanism
Locking the talocrural joint in maximal rigid plantarflexion to resist compressive loading forces during initial contact phase
Accelerating the forward propulsion of the body over the metatarsophalangeal joints via concentric calf plantarflexion activation
explanation: The heel rocker uses the calcaneus as a fulcrum: as the heel contacts the ground, the pretibial muscles (tibialis anterior) contract eccentrically to lower the forefoot smoothly while pulling the tibia forward.
source: Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function - Jacquelin Perry & Judith M. Burnfield

text: During the 'Mid-Stance' phase of gait, which muscle group contracts eccentrically to control the forward progression of the tibia over the stationary foot (Second Ankle Rocker)?
options: Tibialis Anterior and Extensor Digitorum Longus anterior musculature
Hamstring muscle group contracting isometrically to extend the hip
Gastrocnemius and Soleus (Plantarflexors) posterior calf complex
Quadriceps Femoris contracting concentrically to hyperextend the knee
explanation: During Mid-Stance (ankle rocker), the soleus and gastrocnemius contract eccentrically to restrain forward tibial momentum, controlling the rate of tibial advancement and stabilizing the knee.
source: Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function - Jacquelin Perry & Judith M. Burnfield

text: A 'Trendelenburg Gait' is characterized by excessive pelvic drop of the unsupported swing limb during single-leg stance, caused by weakness of which muscle on the stance limb?
options: Iliopsoas and Rectus Femoris primary flexor group
Gluteus Maximus and Adductor Magnus extensor group
Tensor Fasciae Latae contracting in total isolation
Gluteus Medius and Gluteus Minimus abductor group
explanation: Weakness of the stance-limb hip abductors (Gluteus Medius/Minimus) prevents adequate stabilization of the pelvis in the frontal plane, causing the contralateral unsupported pelvis to drop during swing.
source: Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function - Jacquelin Perry & Judith M. Burnfield

text: In shoulder kinesiology, what is the normal physiological 'Scapulohumeral Rhythm' ratio during full active arm abduction from 0 to 180 degrees?
options: 2:1 overall ratio (2 degrees of glenohumeral motion for every 1 degree of scapulothoracic upward rotation)
4:1 overall ratio (4 degrees of glenohumeral motion for every 1 degree of clavicular elevation)
1:1 overall ratio (1 degree of glenohumeral motion for every 1 degree of scapulothoracic motion)
3:1 overall ratio (3 degrees of scapulothoracic motion for every 1 degree of glenohumeral elevation)
explanation: During 180° of shoulder abduction, the normal overall ratio is 2:1, consisting of approximately 120° of glenohumeral motion and 60° of scapulothoracic upward rotation.
source: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann / Inman

text: A 'Steppage Gait' (High-Stepping Gait) is a pathological gait adaptation resulting from which neurological deficit?
options: Hamstring muscle weakness causing premature terminal knee extension before contact
Foot drop caused by weakness of ankle dorsiflexors due to Deep Peroneal Nerve palsy
Gastrocnemius spasticity locking the ankle joint in a rigid calcaneus position
Quadriceps femoris contracture preventing knee flexion during mid-swing
explanation: Steppage gait is an exaggerated hip and knee flexion compensation to ensure toe clearance during swing, caused by foot drop resulting from deep peroneal (fibular) nerve lesion or L4/L5 radiculopathy.
source: Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function - Jacquelin Perry & Judith M. Burnfield

text: According to the Pain Gate Control Theory (Melzack & Wall), how does High-Frequency Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation (Conventional TENS at 80–120 Hz) produce analgesia?
options: Directly destroying sensory nerve endings in the epidermis through localized thermal electrocoagulation and high-frequency heating
Selectively stimulating large-diameter myelinated A-beta afferents to inhibit nociceptive transmission at the spinal cord dorsal horn
Selectively depolarizing small unmyelinated C fibers to deplete substance P stores within peripheral sensory cutaneous nerve terminals
Stimulating the pituitary gland to release systemic beta-endorphins into circulating cerebrospinal fluid and peripheral bloodstream
explanation: Conventional TENS (high frequency 80–120 Hz, low pulse duration <100 µs) selectively activates low-threshold, non-nociceptive A-beta fibers, which excite inhibitory interneurons (substantia gelatinosa) in the spinal dorsal horn to close the pain gate to A-delta and C fibers.
source: Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice - Tim Watson

text: In therapeutic ultrasound application, which frequency is clinically selected when targeting deep biological structures such as the piriformis, hip capsule, or patellar tendon?
options: 1 MHz generates pure electrical currents without sound; 3 MHz generates pure acoustic mechanical waves without heating
3 MHz penetrates deeper (up to 5–7 cm) for deep tissues; 1 MHz penetrates superficially (0.5–1 cm) for cutaneous skin layers
1 MHz penetrates deeper (up to 3–5 cm) for deep structures; 3 MHz penetrates superficially (1–2 cm) for superficial structures
1 MHz is used exclusively for bone fractures; 3 MHz is used exclusively for peripheral nerve regeneration in the upper limb
explanation: Ultrasound energy at 1 MHz is absorbed less rapidly in superficial tissues and penetrates deeply (3–5 cm), making it ideal for deep structures, whereas 3 MHz is absorbed superficially (1–2 cm).
source: Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice - Tim Watson

text: In Neuromuscular Electrical Stimulation (NMES) for quadriceps muscle re-education following ACL reconstruction, what parameter settings represent 'Russian Current' (Kots technique)?
options: A rapid thermal coagulation of sensory nociceptors that permanently blocks action potential propagation along peripheral axons
An electrical polarization of the lipid bilayer that forces open voltage-gated calcium channels across the whole muscle belly
A stable cavitation mechanism producing localized acoustic streaming that enhances cell membrane permeability and protein synthesis
A mechanical shear force that dissolves extracellular hydroxyapatite crystals within the deep connective tissue matrix layers
explanation: Russian Current uses a 2500 Hz medium-frequency AC carrier wave modulated into 50 bursts per second (50 Hz burst frequency) with a 10 ms on, 10 ms off burst duration (50% duty cycle), designed to elicit strong muscular contractions.
source: Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice - Tim Watson / Ward

text: In electrotherapy, what is the 'Beam Non-Uniformity Ratio' (BNR) of an ultrasound transducer head, and what is the clinically acceptable standard?
options: The ratio of spatial peak intensity to spatial average intensity, which should be ≤6:1 to prevent localized tissue hot spots
The ratio of piezoelectric crystal surface area to transducer casing circumference, which must precisely equal 2:1
The ratio of acoustic absorption in cortical bone versus subcutaneous adipose tissue, which must consistently exceed 10:1
The ratio of acoustic pulse delivery time to rest pause duration, which should be strictly maintained at a ratio of 1:1
explanation: BNR is the ratio of peak intensity ($I_{SP}$) to average intensity ($I_{SA}$) across the soundhead. High quality transducers have a low BNR (<5:1 or 6:1), minimizing localized hot spots that can cause periosteal pain.
source: Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice - Tim Watson

text: In neuro-rehabilitation, what is the primary therapeutic philosophy of the Bobath concept (Neuro-Developmental Treatment - NDT)?
options: Applying high-resistance strength training exclusively on open-chain variable resistance machines to induce muscular hypertrophy
Immobilizing the non-paretic sound limb in a mitt for 90% of waking hours to force intensive repetitive use of the paretic extremity
Using primitive pathological reflex synergies and associated reactions to initiate gross voluntary movement in flaccid limb stages
Inhibiting abnormal muscle tone and primitive reflexes while facilitating normal postural control and task-specific movement patterns
explanation: The Bobath/NDT concept focuses on normalizing muscle tone, inhibiting abnormal movement synergies and spasticity through handling techniques, and facilitating normal postural alignment and functional motor patterns.
source: Physical Rehabilitation - Susan B. O'Sullivan & Thomas J. Schmitz

text: According to Signe Brunnstrom's stages of stroke motor recovery, what characterizes Stage 3 of hemiplegic motor recovery?
options: Complete flaccidity with zero active reflex or voluntary motor response elicitation
Spasticity reaches its peak and basic movement synergies can be performed voluntarily
Spasticity begins to decline and isolated joint movements outside synergies become possible
Normal motor coordination and individual joint control are restored completely
explanation: Brunnstrom Stage 3 is characterized by peak spasticity and voluntary control of movement synergies (flexion or extension synergies can be initiated voluntarily, but isolated movement is not yet possible).
source: Physical Rehabilitation - Susan B. O'Sullivan & Thomas J. Schmitz / Brunnstrom

text: In neuro-rehabilitation of upper extremity hemiparesis following stroke, what protocol defines Constraint-Induced Movement Therapy (CIMT)?
options: Immobilizing both upper extremities in bilateral rigid plaster casts while performing passive gait re-education on a treadmill
Applying continuous sensory transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation to both upper extremities simultaneously during seated rest
Restraining the involved paretic arm in a static splint while training the sound contralateral limb in bilateral coordination tasks
Constraining the non-paretic upper limb in a mitt for 90% of waking hours while engaging the paretic arm in intensive repetitive training
explanation: CIMT (Taub) involves restraining the unaffected limb (typically 90% of waking hours for 2 weeks) combined with repetitive, intensive task-oriented training of the paretic arm (shaping) to overcome 'learned non-use'.
source: Physical Rehabilitation - Susan B. O'Sullivan & Thomas J. Schmitz / Taub

text: In ataxia rehabilitation, what are 'Frenkel's Exercises' and what sensory modality do they heavily rely on to compensate for proprioceptive loss?
options: Spasticity declines and voluntary movement combinations deviating from synergies emerge (Stage 4)
Individual joint movements become isolated with completely normal motor coordination (Stage 6)
Flaccidity with complete absence of reflex responses or voluntary movement (Stage 1)
Spasticity reaches its peak with voluntary movement limited to basic synergy patterns (Stage 3)
explanation: Frenkel's exercises are a series of slow, precise, repetitive movements (lying, sitting, standing, walking) designed for cerebellar and sensory ataxia that use visual feedback and focused mental concentration to compensate for impaired proprioception.
source: Physical Rehabilitation - Susan B. O'Sullivan & Thomas J. Schmitz / Frenkel

text: In athletic rehabilitation, what is the 'Core Stability' model (Panjabi) comprising three integrated subsystems that maintain spinal stability?
options: Passive subsystem (vertebrae/ligaments), Active subsystem (muscles/tendons), and Neural subsystem (CNS/sensory receptors)
Cardiovascular systemic perfusion, pulmonary alveolar gas exchange, and peripheral neuromuscular motor command pathways
Superficial rectus abdominis sling, lateral external oblique muscular corset, and posterior latissimus dorsi myofascial sling
Thoracic ribcage osseous cage, lumbar lordotic vertebral column, and pelvic ring architectural osseous structural frameworks
explanation: Manohar Panjabi's spinal stability model comprises three interdependent subsystems: the Passive subsystem (vertebrae, discs, ligaments), the Active subsystem (spinal muscles/tendons), and the Neural control subsystem (sensors and CNS).
source: Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques - Carolyn Kisner & Lynn Allen Colby / Panjabi

text: In patellar tendinopathy rehabilitation, why is the 'Decline Squat' on a 25-degree wedge biomechanically superior to a standard flat-ground squat?
options: It eliminates all mechanical ground reaction forces passing through the knee joint axis
It minimizes calf contribution and increases patellar tendon load and quadriceps demand
It shifts weight completely to the gluteus maximus while reducing all quadriceps EMG activity
It forces the knee into extreme varus alignment to unload the lateral femoral condyle
explanation: Squatting on a 25° decline board decreases the ankle dorsiflexion requirement (reducing calf/plantarflexor force) and increases knee extensor moment and quadriceps/patellar tendon tensile load, isolating the tendon for remodeling.
source: Brukner & Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine - Peter Brukner et al. / Purdam et al.

text: In Interferential Therapy (IFT), how is a low-frequency 'beat frequency' (e.g., 100 Hz) produced deep within biological tissues?
options: By applying a high-power monochromatic coherent laser beam synchronized with continuous pulsed shortwave diathermy units
By rapid mechanical vibrations delivered through a focused acoustic piezoelectric crystal transducer onto the joint line
By the spatial intersection and constructive interference of two medium-frequency AC currents (e.g., 4000 Hz and 4100 Hz)
By directly transmitting a high-voltage 100 Hz DC rectangular pulse from one active electrode over the motor point site
explanation: IFT uses two medium-frequency out-of-phase AC currents (e.g., 4000 Hz and 4100 Hz) that pass through the skin with low impedance and cross deep in tissues, producing an amplitude-modulated low-frequency beat frequency (e.g., 100 Hz).
source: Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice - Tim Watson

text: What is the primary physiological rationale for applying 'Iontophoresis' using Dexamethasone Sodium Phosphate in acute sports inflammatory conditions?
options: Using high-frequency alternating current to heat subcutaneous adipose tissue structures
Using a positive anode to repel positively charged calcium ions into deep articular bone
Using a negative cathode to repel negatively charged corticosteroid ions across the stratum corneum
Using direct microcurrent to permanently coagulate superficial cutaneous capillary loops
explanation: Dexamethasone sodium phosphate is a negatively charged corticosteroid molecule. It is placed under the negative electrode (Cathode), which electrostatically repels the like-charged molecules across the skin into local tissues.
source: Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice - Tim Watson

text: In neurorehabilitation, how is 'spasticity' differentiated clinically from 'rigidity' during passive movement assessment?
options: Spasticity occurs exclusively in cerebellar vermis lesions; Rigidity occurs exclusively in lower motor neuron anterior horn lesions
Spasticity is velocity-dependent with a clasp-knife resistance; Rigidity is velocity-independent with constant resistance throughout range
Spasticity affects exclusively distal wrist flexor muscles; Rigidity affects exclusively cranial nerve innervated facial muscles
Spasticity is velocity-independent lead-pipe resistance; Rigidity is velocity-dependent increasing only during rapid ballistic stretching
explanation: Spasticity is a velocity-dependent increase in tonic stretch reflexes (UMN lesion / pyramidal tract) often exhibiting a clasp-knife phenomenon. Rigidity (extrapyramidal / Parkinson's) is velocity-independent and uniform (lead-pipe or cogwheel).
source: Physical Rehabilitation - Susan B. O'Sullivan & Thomas J. Schmitz

text: In cervical spine physical assessment, what constitutes a positive 'Spurling's Test' (Foraminal Compression Test) for cervical radiculopathy?
options: Resisted isometric neck extension producing generalized muscular fatigue and dull aching in the upper trapezius muscle
Passive lateral flexion and axial downward compression reproducing radicular pain into the ipsilateral upper extremity
Passive neck flexion causing sharp electric-like shocks shooting down the spinal cord and into the lower extremities
Passive bilateral cervical rotation reproducing localized dizziness, rotary nystagmus, and unilateral Horner syndrome
explanation: Spurling's test (cervical side-bending, slight extension, and axial compression) narrows the neural foramina, reproducing familiar radicular radiating arm pain, with high specificity (>92%) for cervical nerve root compression.
source: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee / Wainner et al.

text: The 'Ober's Test' evaluates contracture or tightness of which lower extremity anatomical soft-tissue structure?
options: Semitendinosus and Semimembranosus medial hamstring group
Gastrocnemius and Soleus deep posterior compartment
Iliotibial Band (ITB) and Tensor Fasciae Latae (TFL)
Rectus Femoris and Iliopsoas anterior muscle complex
explanation: Ober's test (patient side-lying, tested hip extended and abducted, then allowed to drop into adduction) evaluates contracture of the Iliotibial Band (ITB) and Tensor Fasciae Latae (TFL). Failure of the knee to adduct past table horizontal is positive.
source: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee

text: The 'Thompson Test' (Simmonds' Squeeze Test) is diagnostic for complete rupture of the Achilles tendon when:
options: Passive dorsiflexion of the ankle reproduces localized paresthesia over the first webspace
Squeezing the calf muscle belly in prone position elicits brisk passive ankle plantarflexion
Resisted active plantarflexion produces severe clicking over the anterior tibiofibular mortise
Squeezing the calf muscle belly in prone position fails to elicit passive plantarflexion of the foot
explanation: In Thompson's (Simmonds') test, squeezing the calf of a prone patient with feet hanging free normally elicits mechanical ankle plantarflexion. Absence of foot movement indicates complete disruption of the Achilles tendon.
source: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee

text: In the foot and ankle, what physical examination maneuver constitutes the 'Windlass Test' for Plantar Fasciitis?
options: Applying direct downward axial percussion over the anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament
Passive hyperextension of the First Metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint while the athlete is weight-bearing
Resisting active eversion of the subtalar joint with the foot held in maximal dorsiflexion
Forceful passive inversion and plantarflexion of the entire foot while palpating the lateral malleolus
explanation: The Windlass test involves passive dorsiflexion of the first MTP joint with the athlete weight-bearing (or non-weight-bearing), pulling the plantar fascia tight around the metatarsal head; reproduction of heel pain is diagnostic for plantar fasciitis.
source: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee

text: When performing the 'Thomas Test' for hip flexor flexibility, if the extended thigh remains elevated off the examination table while the knee flexes to 90 degrees, and extending the knee allows the thigh to drop flat, the tightness is localized to:
options: Pectineus and Adductor Longus (anteromedial hip flexor group)
Iliopsoas muscle belly (deep primary hip flexor muscle group)
Rectus Femoris muscle (two-joint hip flexor / knee extensor)
Tensor Fasciae Latae (lateral hip flexor and abductor unit)
explanation: In the modified Thomas test, if the thigh touches the table when the knee is extended (slackening the two-joint rectus femoris across the knee) but rises when the knee is flexed to 90°, isolated Rectus Femoris contracture is confirmed.
source: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee

text: What is the physiological mechanism behind the 'Hunting Reaction' (Lewis reaction) observed during prolonged local cryotherapy application?
options: Continuous progressive vasoconstriction leading to severe tissue hypoxia, cellular necrosis, and cold-induced ischemia
Permanent dilation of deep muscular arteries with rapid increase in local tissue temperature and cellular metabolic rate
Immediate reflex inhibition of all cutaneous sensory thermoreceptors and complete blockade of motor nerve transmission
Cyclic alternating periods of cold-induced vasodilation following initial vasoconstriction to preserve tissue viability
explanation: Lewis' Hunting Reaction is a transient cold-induced vasodilation (CIVD) occurring after prolonged cooling (>15–20 min at <10°C), mediated by axon reflexes or neurotransmitter depletion, serving as a protective mechanism against local tissue freezing.
source: Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice - Tim Watson

text: The 'FADIR Test' (Flexion, Adduction, Internal Rotation) of the hip is the primary physical assessment screening test for:
options: Femoroacetabular Impingement (FAI) and Anterior Acetabular Labral Tears
Trochanteric pain syndrome and gluteus medius insertional tendinopathy
Posterior hip dislocation and piriformis sciatic nerve compression
Ischial bursitis and hamstring proximal origin avulsion tears
explanation: The FADIR test (Flexion, ADduction, Internal Rotation) jams the femoral neck against the anterosuperior acetabular labrum. Reproduction of groin pain has high sensitivity (>95%) for FAI and anterior labral tears.
source: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee

text: Case Vignette 1: A 24-year-old international track sprinter clutched his posterior right thigh during maximal velocity sprinting in the final 20 meters of a 100m race. On physical examination at 24 hours post-injury, there is focal tenderness 6 cm distal to the ischial tuberosity along the biceps femoris muscle belly, pain with resisted knee flexion at 30 degrees, and an inability to perform a single-leg bridge without sharp pain. MRI confirms a Grade 2 muscle-tendon junction strain of the Biceps Femoris long head. According to the British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC), what anatomical classification code corresponds to a moderate muscle strain at the myotendinous junction?
options: Grade 3c (extensive intratendinous / aponeurosis rupture)
Grade 2b (moderate myotendinous junction structural tear)
Grade 4 (complete muscle or tendon avulsion disruption)
Grade 1a (minor localized myofascial muscle strain injury)
explanation: The BAMIC classification grades muscle injuries by severity (0–4) and anatomical site: 'a' = myofascial (peripheral), 'b' = myotendinous junction (classic), 'c' = intratendinous (central tendon/aponeurosis). A moderate MTJ tear is Grade 2b.
source: Brukner & Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine - Peter Brukner et al. / Pollock et al.

text: Case Vignette 1 (Continued): As the sports performance analyst and physiotherapist designing this sprinter's criteria-based rehabilitation progression, which exercise represents the essential evidence-based modality to restore eccentric fascicle length and prevent recurrence?
options: Low-intensity continuous stationary cycling exclusively at zero magnetic resistance for 8 consecutive weeks
Passive static hamstring stretching on a massage table for 15 minutes daily throughout the competitive season
Seated light leg extensions performed on a variable resistance machine to muscular fatigue twice every week
Nordic Hamstring Exercise with progressive eccentric overload and structured high-speed sprinting exposures
explanation: The Nordic Hamstring Exercise provides supramaximal eccentric stimulus at long muscle lengths, driving sarcomerogenesis (increasing Biceps Femoris fascicle length) and significantly reducing reinjury rates when paired with progressive sprinting.
source: Brukner & Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine - Peter Brukner et al. / Petersen et al.

text: Case Vignette 2: A 22-year-old elite cricket fast bowler reports progressive posterior shoulder pain and a sensation of 'dead arm' during the late cocking and release phases of bowling. On clinical examination, dominant shoulder external rotation (ER) is 125 degrees (contralateral 100 degrees), but internal rotation (IR) is only 35 degrees (contralateral 65 degrees). The Total Arc of Motion is 160 degrees in the dominant arm compared to 165 degrees in the non-dominant arm. The athlete demonstrates a Glenohumeral Internal Rotation Deficit (GIRD) of 30 degrees. What is the clinical significance of a GIRD exceeding 20 degrees with a Total Arc deficit of >5 degrees in throwing athletes?
options: It represents a benign physiological bone adaptation requiring zero physical intervention
It is a significant risk factor for superior labral (SLAP) tears and internal impingement
It confirms complete severance of the axillary nerve within the quadrangular space
It indicates an acute structural fracture of the anatomical neck of the proximal humerus
explanation: Pathological GIRD (loss of IR >18–20° accompanied by a Total Arc deficit >5°) alters glenohumeral kinematics during cocking, increasing superior/posterior labral shear and significantly elevating risk for SLAP lesions and cuff tears.
source: Brukner & Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine - Peter Brukner et al. / Wilk et al.

text: Case Vignette 2 (Continued): Which targeted physiotherapeutic stretching intervention is most effective for addressing the posterior capsular and rotator cuff tightness in this fast bowler?
options: Restoring full symmetrical passive knee extension (0°) immediately within the first 1 to 2 weeks post-operatively
Initiating heavy open-chain quadriceps leg extensions from 90° to 0° with maximal loads on post-operative day one
Immobilizing the knee in 45° of flexion in a rigid plaster cast for six consecutive weeks without weight-bearing
Achieving 140° of deep knee flexion within the first 48 hours post-operatively using high-force passive stretching
explanation: The Sleeper stretch and cross-body stretch with scapular stabilization specifically stretch the posterior-inferior capsule and posterior rotator cuff (infraspinatus/teres minor), effectively restoring internal rotation in throwing athletes.
source: Brukner & Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine - Peter Brukner et al. / McClure et al.

text: Case Vignette 3: A 21-year-old elite female badminton player felt a sudden 'pop' in her right knee during a rapid change-of-direction landing on the court. Immediate hemarthrosis developed within 2 hours. Physical examination reveals a positive Lachman test with a soft end-feel and a positive Pivot-Shift test. MRI confirms an acute mid-substance tear of the Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL). Which anatomical structure is most commonly subjected to concomitant bone contusions ('kissing contusions') during the classic valgus-internal rotation ACL injury mechanism?
options: Medial malleolus groove and talar dome anteromedial articular cartilage surface
Superior patellar pole and anterior femoral trochlear groove apex articular rim
Lateral femoral condyle (terminal sulcus) and posterior lateral tibial plateau
Medial femoral condyle (intercondylar ridge) and anterior medial tibial plateau
explanation: During acute non-contact ACL rupture, the tibia subluxates anteriorly while the knee is in valgus and internal rotation, causing violent impaction between the posterior lateral tibial plateau and the lateral femoral condyle ('kissing contusions').
source: Brukner & Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine - Peter Brukner et al.

text: Case Vignette 3 (Continued): The athlete undergoes bone-patellar tendon-bone (BPTB) autograft ACL reconstruction. During early Phase 1 (Weeks 0–4) rehabilitation, what is the primary clinical priority to prevent arthrofibrosis and long-term patellofemoral complications?
options: Anteromedial bundle of the Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) and transverse ligament
Posterolateral Corner (PLC) complex (FCL, popliteus tendon, popliteofibular ligament)
Superficial Medial Collateral Ligament (sMCL) and posterior oblique ligament (POL)
Medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL) and medial patellotibial ligament complex
explanation: Restoring full passive knee extension (symmetrical to contralateral hyperextension) in early Phase 1 is the critical milestone post-ACL reconstruction to prevent cyclops lesions, arthrofibrosis, quadriceps shut-down, and patellofemoral pain.
source: Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques - Carolyn Kisner & Lynn Allen Colby / Shelbourne

text: Case Vignette 4: A 29-year-old competitive tennis player reports lateral elbow pain aggravated during one-handed backhand strokes. Palpation demonstrates focal tenderness 1 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle. Resisted wrist extension with the elbow in extension and resisted middle finger extension (Maudsley's test) reproduce familiar pain. What is the most likely underlying structural pathology?
options: Radial head acute undisplaced structural stress fracture with hematoma
Ulnar collateral ligament anterior bundle ligamentous sprain at the elbow
Medial epicondyle common flexor-pronator tendon micro-tear lesion
Tendinopathy of the Extensor Carpi Radialis Brevis (ECRB) tendon origin
explanation: Lateral epicondylalgia ('Tennis Elbow') is characterized by tenderness over the ECRB origin, pain with resisted wrist extension in elbow extension, and a positive Maudsley's test (resisted middle finger extension stressing ECRB/EDC).
source: Brukner & Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine - Peter Brukner et al.

text: Case Vignette 4 (Continued): In rehabilitating this athlete's lateral epicondylalgia, which progressive loading exercise utilizing a flexible rubber bar (Tyler Twist) or dumbbell has shown strong clinical efficacy?
options: Complete wrist splint immobilization for three months with absolute rest
Isolated passive wrist flexion stretching without any active resistance loading
Eccentric-concentric wrist extensor loading with progressive mechanical resistance
High-frequency wrist pronation drills performed continuously to muscular exhaustion
explanation: The Tyler Twist (using a FlexBar) and progressive eccentric-concentric wrist extensor strengthening promote tendon remodeling, upregulate collagen synthesis, and restore mechanical load tolerance in lateral epicondylalgia.
source: Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques - Carolyn Kisner & Lynn Allen Colby / Tyler et al.

text: Case Vignette 5: An 18-year-old competitive soccer player suffered an acute inversion ankle trauma. Physical examination reveals swelling and exquisite tenderness over the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) and calcaneofibular ligament (CFL). The anterior drawer test is positive for laxity. Plain radiographs rule out fracture according to the Ottawa Ankle Rules. What is the Ottawa Ankle Rule criteria that mandates an ankle X-ray series following acute trauma?
options: Inability to perform a single-leg heel raise without assistance within 24 hours of the acute inversion ankle injury
Bone tenderness along the distal 6 cm of the posterior edge of either malleolus or inability to bear weight for 4 steps
Presence of superficial cutaneous ecchymosis and localized soft tissue swelling over the dorsal surface of the midfoot
Severe sharp pain during active inversion and eversion of the subtalar joint in non-weight-bearing sitting position
explanation: The Ottawa Ankle Rules mandate radiographs if there is bone tenderness along the posterior edge/tip of the distal 6 cm of the lateral or medial malleolus, OR an inability to bear weight for four steps both immediately and in the ED.
source: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee / Stiell et al.

text: Case Vignette 5 (Continued): Following resolution of acute pain and swelling in this soccer player, which functional training component is most critical to prevent chronic ankle instability and recurrent sprains?
options: Passive non-weight-bearing bed rest and immobilization in a rigid plaster cast for six consecutive months
Progressive multi-directional dynamic balance, proprioceptive wobble-board training, and reactive perturbation drills
Daily application of superficial ice packs and continuous passive motion without any active exercise therapy
High-velocity manual manipulation of the subtalar joint delivered into forced inversion at end-range
explanation: Level 1 evidence strongly supports sensorimotor, wobble-board, perturbation, and dynamic balance training (e.g., Star Excursion / Y-Balance) to restore peroneal reaction time and prevent recurrent ankle sprains.
source: Brukner & Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine - Peter Brukner et al. / International Ankle Consortium

text: Case Vignette 6: A 12-year-old junior competitive football player reports bilateral posterior heel pain during and after sprint drills. On physical examination, there is exquisite pain on the Calcaneal Squeeze Test (compressing medial and lateral calcaneal walls), reduced ankle dorsiflexion range (5° with knee straight), and tight gastrocnemius-soleus complex. What is the diagnosis?
options: Bicipital tenosynovitis within the bicipital groove of the proximal humerus
Adhesive capsulitis of the glenohumeral joint with global capsular restriction
Subacromial subdeltoid bursitis with localized subacromial impingement syndrome
Full-thickness rotator cuff tendon tear or severe axillary nerve palsy (deltoid paralysis)
explanation: Sever's disease (calcaneal apophysitis) is a traction osteochondrosis of the secondary calcaneal ossification center caused by repetitive Achilles tendon pull in growing children (ages 8–12), diagnosed by a positive Calcaneal Squeeze test.
source: Brukner & Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine - Peter Brukner et al.

text: Case Vignette 6 (Continued): What is the most appropriate initial physiotherapy management plan for this young athlete with Sever's disease?
options: High-impact plyometric jumping drills performed daily on hard concrete surfaces
Load modification, temporary heel lifts/cushions, and gentle calf stretching/strengthening
Immediate surgical excision of the calcaneal apophysis under general anesthesia
Complete bed rest and permanent cessation of all future youth sports participation
explanation: Sever's is benign and self-limiting, resolving completely once the calcaneal growth plate ossifies (~14–15 yrs). Education and reassurance alleviate parent anxiety, managed simply with load modification and heel lifts.
source: Brukner & Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine - Peter Brukner et al. / Scharfbillig et al.

text: Case Vignette 7: A 20-year-old elite female distance runner presents with insidious, aching pain along the posteromedial border of the distal third of the tibia, covering a diffuse area of approximately 6 cm. Symptoms are worst at the beginning of running, ease as she warms up, but ache persistently after workouts. There is no focal cortical tenderness. What is the clinical diagnosis?
options: Complete rupture of the flexor hallucis longus tendon sheath at ankle
Chronic Exertional Compartment Syndrome of the anterior deep compartment
Medial Tibial Stress Syndrome (MTSS / 'Shin Splints' - Traction Periostitis)
Anterior Tibial Cortex High-Risk Stress Fracture with cortical lucency
explanation: Medial Tibial Stress Syndrome (MTSS) presents as diffuse posteromedial tibial border tenderness (typically ≥5 cm) that warms up with exercise, representing traction periostitis at the fascial attachments (soleus/tibialis posterior).
source: Brukner & Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine - Peter Brukner et al. / Moen et al.
