text: Case Vignette 7 (Continued): If this runner's symptoms had shown focal pinpoint tenderness over the anterior tibial cortex with severe night pain and pain on single-leg hopping, which imaging modality is gold standard to confirm a suspected bone stress injury?
options: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) total body regional composition scan
Plain lateral radiograph performed immediately within 24 hours of symptom onset
Diagnostic therapeutic ultrasound scanning of the superficial subcutaneous soft tissue
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) showing bone marrow edema and periosteal signal
explanation: MRI is the imaging gold standard for bone stress injuries (Fredericson classification), demonstrating intramedullary bone marrow edema and periosteal edema weeks before cortical lucencies appear on plain radiographs.
source: Brukner & Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine - Peter Brukner et al. / Fredericson et al.

text: Case Vignette 8: A 26-year-old professional basketball center presents with localized inferior patellar pole pain for four months. Symptoms are sharp when landing from jumps and during deep squats. Ultrasound imaging demonstrates tendon thickening and hypoechoic areas with hypervascularity (neovascularization) on power Doppler at the deep proximal patellar tendon origin. What is the primary histological characteristic of this condition (Patellar Tendinopathy)?
options: Non-inflammatory cell-mediated degenerative tendinosis with collagen disruption and hypervascularity
Complete mechanical severance of the deep insertional fibers of the rectus femoris tendon
Massive acute inflammatory cell infiltration dominated by active polymorphonuclear neutrophils
Acute pyogenic bacterial infection of the subpatellar infrapatellar fat pad synovial space
explanation: Cook and Purdam's continuum model confirms that chronic tendinopathies are not inflammatory 'tendinitis', but rather cell-mediated 'tendinosis' characterized by tenocyte rounding, ground substance increase, collagen disorganization, and neovascular ingrowth.
source: Brukner & Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine - Peter Brukner et al. / Cook & Purdam

text: Case Vignette 8 (Continued): In designing the initial in-season rehabilitation loading protocol for this basketball player with severe patellar tendon pain (VAS 7/10), which exercise intervention provides immediate cortical-mediated pain relief (tendon neuroplastic modulation)?
options: Rapid ballistic concentric knee extensions performed on an isokinetic dynamometer to exhaustion
Passive continuous bed rest with strict avoidance of all lower extremity weight-bearing movements
High-load isometric quadriceps contractions (e.g., Spanish Squat / leg press held at 60° for 45s x 5 reps)
High-velocity drop jumps from a 60 cm plyometric box onto hard flooring surfaces without warm-up
explanation: Rio et al. demonstrated that heavy isometric loading (5 sets of 45s holds @ 70% MVC) produces immediate analgesia lasting 45+ minutes and reduces cortical motor inhibition in patellar tendinopathy.
source: Brukner & Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine - Peter Brukner et al. / Rio et al.

text: Case Vignette 9: During video-based motion analysis of a drop-vertical jump in a female volleyball athlete, the analyst observes marked dynamic knee valgus (medial knee collapse), hip adduction, and internal rotation upon landing under fatigue. Which biomechanical and muscular deficit is primarily responsible for this uncontrolled landing mechanic?
options: Excessive tensile stiffness and structural tightness of the posterior cruciate ligament
Weakness and delayed neuromuscular firing of the Gluteus Medius and hip external rotators
Increased ankle dorsiflexion range of motion extending beyond 45 degrees of flexion
Hypertrophy and excessive explosive force production of the gastrocnemius muscle
explanation: Dynamic knee valgus collapse during jump-landing is primarily driven by proximal hip muscle deficits (weakness and delayed activation of gluteus medius and maximus), leading to excessive femoral adduction and internal rotation.
source: Brukner & Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine - Peter Brukner et al. / Hewett et al.

text: Case Vignette 9 (Continued): Which specific targeted training intervention should be implemented to correct this athlete's dynamic knee valgus landing pattern?
options: Forceful high-velocity manipulation of the radiohumeral joint delivered into forced extension and pronation
Immobilizing the elbow, forearm, and wrist in a long-arm fiberglass cast for twelve consecutive weeks
Isolated eccentric contractions of the wrist extensors (Extensor Carpi Radialis Brevis) using the flexible bar
Continuous application of ultrasound at 3 W/cm2 delivered directly over the radial nerve superficial branch
explanation: Evidence-based injury prevention programs (e.g., FIFA 11+, Sportsmetrics) use neuromuscular jump-landing retraining (soft landings, knee over toes), augmented feedback, and progressive hip abductor/core strengthening to eliminate valgus collapse.
source: Brukner & Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine - Peter Brukner et al. / Myer et al.

text: Case Vignette 10: An 18-year-old cricket fast bowler presents with acute-on-chronic focal low back pain on his non-bowling arm side, exacerbated during the front-foot contact and delivery stride. On examination, extension and ipsilateral rotation reproduce sharp localized pain, and the single-leg hyperextension (Stork standing) test is strongly positive. What is the primary suspected diagnosis?
options: Lumbar Spondylolysis (stress fracture of the pars interarticularis)
Sacroiliac joint anterior displacement and ligamentous disruption
Acute thoracic disc herniation with severe spinal cord compression
Sciatic nerve entrapment within the piriformis muscle belly
explanation: In adolescent and young fast bowlers, extension and rotation loading during front-foot contact places massive hyperextension/rotation stress on the contralateral pars interarticularis, frequently causing active spondylolysis.
source: Brukner & Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine - Peter Brukner et al.

text: Case Vignette 10 (Continued): What is the core rehabilitation priority in the conservative management of this young fast bowler with active spondylolysis?
options: High-velocity spinal manipulative thrusts delivered directly into painful hyperextension to forcefully mobilize the lumbar facet joints
Aggressive hyperextension spinal stretches and continuous heavy bowling drills performed daily throughout the active competitive season
Relative rest from aggravating extension/rotation loads, deep lumbo-pelvic core stabilization in neutral spine, and gradual reconditioning
Complete absolute bed rest for six consecutive months with strict avoidance of all physical activity and spinal stabilization exercises
explanation: Active pars stress lesions require relative rest from aggravating extension/rotation (typically 8–12 weeks), neutral-spine core stabilization (multifidus, transversus abdominis), correction of bowling biomechanics, and gradual load progression.
source: Brukner & Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine - Peter Brukner et al. / Engstrom et al.
